## Abstract

The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory will complete its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in the mid-2030s. Its 8.4 m aperture and 9.6 deg2 field of view give it an étendue unmatched by any facility planned for that era. The Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop (KIPAC/SLAC, 3–5 August 2026) brought together $\sim$ 100 participants to ask . This paper summarizes the workshop’s structure and discussions. Five working groups considered continued LSST-style surveying; alternative cadences and footprints; new filters; targets of opportunity and multi-messenger astronomy; and enabling technologies and upgrades. The continued-surveying group explored for detection, deblending, and classification in the faint, crowded sky. The cadence group described a process for allocating post-LSST observing time, along with cadences for a transiting-exoplanet census, Type Ia supernova cosmology, time-delay cosmography, and second-scale transients. The filter group explored offset broadband, medium-band, and narrowband filters for photometric redshifts, high-redshift large-scale structure, AGN reverberation mapping, Galactic archaeology, and emission-line imaging. The multi-messenger group explored target-of-opportunity follow-up of next-generation gravitational-wave and neutrino sources, including standard sirens, kilonovae, and Galactic supernovae. The technology group organized instrumental options by cost and lead time, from configuration changes such as fast readout modes to moderate upgrades such as new filters, a faster shutter, and summit edge computing. Cross-cutting topics included AI/ML, Chilean and Latin-American co-leadership, satellite megaconstellations, and weather and long-term climate trends at Cerro Pachón. The working groups’ white papers are available through the workshop’s Zenodo community (https://zenodo.org/communities/rubin2036workshop/) and the workshop website, which also includes workshop talks (https://rubin-observatory.github.io/Rubin-Beyond-LSST/pages/Rubin2036proceedings/).

## I Introduction

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory was designed and built to carry out the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST): a decade-long, optical survey of the southern sky in six broad photometric bands ( $ugrizy$ ) [23, 9]. The four science pillars of the LSST are probing dark energy and dark matter, taking an inventory of the Solar System, exploring the transient sky, and mapping the formation and structure of the Milky Way. The LSST began in 2026, and by the mid-2030s the nominal ten-year survey will be complete, delivering an unprecedented $\sim$ 18,000 deg2. The telescope, camera, data-management system, and the software will remain one the most capable wide-field imaging worldwide.

This paper summarizes the outcomes of the Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop11 1 https://rubin-observatory.github.io/Rubin-Beyond-LSST/ held at the Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology (KIPAC)22 2 A joint institute of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and Stanford University. on 3–5 August 2026. It presents for Rubin operations beyond the LSST, built on concrete science cases that the community could develop for upcoming prioritization processes, including the next decadal survey in astronomy and astrophysics (Astro2030).

The scientific cases for Rubin rely on its unique étendue ( $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ , the product of collecting area and field of view). No facility planned for the 2030s will match Rubin’s combination of an 8.4 m aperture and a 9.6 deg2 field of view. Other imaging and spectroscopic facilities, such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the 4-meter Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST), the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Roman), and Euclid, will provide complementary capabilities. By the mid-2030s we will also have of data products and scientific discoveries enabled by the LSST itself.

Continuing to operate and evolve a built facility a high-return use of resources: the marginal cost of new capability is small relative both to the cost already committed and to any new facility of comparable reach.

Over the past decade a series of community studies has argued for planning Rubin’s use beyond the LSST, from the Cosmic Visions Dark Energy reports [18, 19, 17], through Astro2020 white papers on next-generation LSST science and future uses of the facility [24, 26], the LSST next-generation instrumentation workshop [34], dedicated narrow-band filter studies [36], and the Snowmass 2021 process [12, 21, 6] (see Appendix D for a summary of previous work). The Astro2020 decadal survey, Pathways to Discovery in Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 2020s [31] set the current scientific priorities for the fieldrecommendations are now the subject of a National Academies mid-decadal review of progress [32], and positions the community to bring well-developed science cases to the next decadal survey (Astro2030).

The workshop brought together approximately 100 in-person and online participants to begin developing this roadmap. A program of invited framing talks on the first day and synergy talks on the second (Appendix B), together with short talks (Appendix C), introduced the scientific, programmatic, and cross-facility context and seeded many of the science cases; slides for a subset are available on the workshop website. The bulk of the time was devoted to collaborative work in five thematic groups: (A) continued LSST-style surveying (Section II); (B) alternative cadences and footprints (Section III); (C) narrow- and medium-band surveys and alternative filters (Section IV); (D) targets of opportunity and multi-messenger astronomy (Section V); and (E) enabling technology and upgrades (Section VI). Each group developed and compared science cases against a common set of prompts, reproduced in full in Appendix Athe specific science goal and the single result that would ; why Rubin, and why cannot wait, framed around its area $\times$ field-of-view ( $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ ); the strongest skeptic’s objection and a rebuttal; the concrete change required (filter set, cadence, instrument, or software) and its lead time; which early-LSST data release must be in hand ; the success metric and figure of merit ; connections to other facilities, surveys, and groups; and the single most useful next step. Two cross-cutting perspectives, the role of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) and opportunities for Latin-American, particularly Chilean, co-leadership (Section VII), were considered across all cases. Other cross-cutting topics, such as satellite megaconstellations and climate-related degradation of seeing, emerged organically during the meeting. The themes were informed by discussions within the Scientific Organizing Committee, participant input during registration, and the previous community efforts noted above.

Each thematic group developed its results into a standalone document, archived in the workshop’s Zenodo community; these are listed in Table 1 and cited at the start of each group’s section below, and the present paper is a summary that points to them for full detail.

## II Group A: Continued LSST-style Surveying

Contributors: P. Yadav. See Yadav [35] for the full Group A document.

Group A considered continuing to survey with the current system beyond the nominal ten years, gaining scientific reach from a longer time baseline, and deeper coadds rather than from any new hardware . Its case argues that the deeper, more crowded imaging a continued survey produces can only be exploited if the detection, deblending, and classification software evolves in step, an argument for sustained investment in rather than in the itself.

### II.1 A survey-native foundation model for the faint, crowded sky

A continued, deepening survey if its faint, crowded sky can actually be measured, and at those depths the fraction of blended detections rises steeply while the availability of vetted training labels does not. The central question is whether a survey-native foundation model (a backbone pretrained self-supervised on Rubin’s own unlabeled $ugrizy$ coadds) can deliver scene-level detection, deblending, and star/galaxy classification at the faint end using only a small fraction of the labels that supervised training requires. The single result that would matter is matching fully supervised performance from roughly 5–15% of the labels, making a scene-level catalog deployable across the whole footprint rather than only in the handful of spectroscopically rich deep fields. The $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ argument here is two-sided: the same survey depth that drives fields into the blended regime (where morphology-only star/galaxy separation degrades to $\sim$ 50% correctly classified injected stars at $i=23.8$ in Data Preview 1 (DP1) source-injection tests) also guarantees that unlabeled pixels, unlike vetted labels, scale exactly with $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ . Evidence from the first application of the DeepDISC scene-level framework to real LSST DP1 imaging (1,458 six-band tiles over the Extended Chandra Deep Field South and the Euclid Deep Field South; 288,277 objects, validated against the Hubble Space Telescope and the Cosmic Assembly Near-infrared Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey) shows scene-level inference reaching 94.8%/71.4% galaxy/star recall against HST (near-parity with a photometry-based random forest) while achieving 94.6% catalog purity on a held-out HST footprint versus 77.6% for the Scarlet-based production pipeline on the same sky. The requirement is not telescope time but infrastructure: sustained GPU compute and bulk-image access for data-release-scale pretraining ( $\sim$ 2–3 yr to stand up), a deep-field truth program (source-injection plus curated spectroscopic/astrometric labels, coordinated with DESI/4MOST), and an integration path to release scene-level catalogs as supported value-added data products. The priors, rerunning the $i=23.8$ injection benchmark with image-based classifiers and , are obtainable from Data Preview 2 (DP2) and . This case , connecting to Roman (joint pixel-level training cuts the simulated unrecognized-blend fraction from 18.6% to 11.6%), Euclid, DESI and , and to Groups B (which deep fields exist to train on), C (photo-z quality is bounded by blended-photometry quality), D (host identification in crowded fields), and E (compute/software infrastructure). A Chilean co-leadership tie-in was proposed around the truth/label program and a data-science training-school module.

## III Group B: Alternative Cadences and Footprints

Contributors: H. Best, S. Birrer, R. Blum, A. S. Bolton, R. Bonito, R. C. Chen, S. Corley, S. Digel, S. Erickson, C. E. Holt, S. Jha, A. I. Malz, P. Marshall, P. Sharma, A. S. Tramuto, L. Venuti, W. M. Wood-Vasey, P. Yadav; and Chilean co-leads T. Anguita and V. Motta. See Birrer and others [10] for the full Group B document.

Group B addressed how to re-tune Rubin’s observing strategy after LSST (e.g., denser cadence, mini- and sub-surveys, monitoring programs, and target-of-opportunity splits) to reach science that the homogeneous, compromise-driven main-survey cadence cannot. Group B participants also identified a “metacase” for the workshop at large: a proposal that the community establish a flexible, prioritized process for allocating post-LSST observing time, rather than commit now to a single fixed alternative cadence. Around that umbrella the group developed a set of concrete science-driven cadences.

### III.1 The metacase: a process for the post-LSST science portfolio

The observation motivating the metacase is that Rubin’s capabilities are not exhausted by the LSST survey design: survey-cadence proposals have consistently oversubscribed the available LSST time, and new ideas as the survey progresses. Because cadence and footprint changes have (shorter than filters or focal-plane hardware), they . What Rubin needs is a survey-strategy framework that can run concurrent programs of differing scale, area, filter set, exposure time, and cadence, together with a scientific prioritization process, modeled on the large/medium/small proposal structure used at other observatories (e.g., Roman’s mix of core community surveys and proposal-based general-astrophysics surveys). The counterargument that the LSST cadence was already optimized in a community process is answered by noting that the most important science in 2036 will differ from the original LSST science goals, and that the main survey necessarily compromised across all cases rather than serving finely targeted ones. Success would be measured by the number and oversubscription of proposals received and by the breadth of community participation; a Chilean tie-in (reserved Chilean-community time or a Chilean Time Allocation Committee, TAC) is a natural component. The metacase is the umbrella under which most Group B, and several cross-group, cases sit.

### III.2 Science-driven cadences

The group developed several cases that such a process would prioritize:

#### Transiting-exoplanet census of the Milky Way disk

A census of transiting planets across all spectral types in the Galactic disk, confirming candidates through $\geq 3$ transits, over $\sim$ 3,600 deg2 of the disk. It requires operational flexibility rather than hardware: . Kepler (0.25% of sky) and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS; bright stars, $r\lesssim 12$ ) leave most of the disk’s planet population unprobed; a benchmark target is confirming planets around $\geq$ 10,000 disk stars.

#### Young stellar objects across all timescales

A multi-band ( $ugriz$ ), high-cadence (30-minute), short-duration ( $\sim$ 10-day) sub-survey of thousands of young stellar objects (YSOs) in several star-forming regions of Rubin’s Galactic footprint would link short-term accretion bursts to long-term eruptive events such as those of EXor-type stars (young stars that undergo repeated months-to-years-long accretion outbursts). Exploiting Rubin’s étendue and its blue and red filters, it would recover light-curve morphologies, determine stellar photospheric properties, and characterize accretion physics as a function of stellar age and environment. Its complementarity with the low-cadence, multi-year LSST view uniquely constrains the occurrence rates of small- versus large-scale events in the accretion histories of young stars, extending the YSO micro-survey already proposed for the LSST [13].

#### Type Ia supernova cosmology to $z\sim 1.1$

A dedicated sub-survey drilling into non-Deep-Drilling-Field regions to fill the Hubble diagram out to $z\sim 1.1$ , where the ten-year LSST sample is sparse, tests of time-varying dark energy beyond $(w_{0},w_{a})$ and tests of cosmic isotropy along continuous sightlines. It needs no new filters; Group C’s offset filters would most benefit this case by preserving discovery depth. Mid-to-late-release cosmology results are the prior that would set the strategy.

#### Strongly-lensed AGN and supernovae for time-delay cosmography

Daily cadence on $\sim$ 2,000 deg2, preferentially on the Roman high-latitude footprint, to measure time delays of lensed quasars and the rare, rapidly-fading lensed supernovae. Concrete performance metrics include accretion-disk sizes measured to 10%, a $5\sigma$ discrimination , and 1% $H_{0}$ from each of the lensed-SN and lensed active-galactic-nucleus (AGN) samples.

#### The few-second sky: ultracompact binaries and fast transients

Two cases exploit second-scale cadence. A fast-cadence Galactic survey (1–2 s continuous imaging over an hour, repeated over years) targets Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA)-era eclipsing double white dwarfs with sub-15-minute periods, comparing the optically-timed orbital decay $\dot{P}$ against the gravitational-wave (GW)-driven prediction to isolate tidal dissipation and test whether such binaries are calibrated GW sirens, a measurement whose precision scales as $\sim T^{-5/2}$ , so . A complementary extragalactic case targets fast blue optical transients and fast-radio-burst (FRB) counterparts, which are washed out in a standard 30 s visit and require 1–2 s readouts plus second-scale alerting. Both depend on enabling technology from Group E (fast readout modes).

#### Solar-System and coordinated-observing mini-surveys

An ecliptic-restricted, daily-cadence mini-survey pairing $g$ and $r$ within each visit would catch the rise of cometary and active-asteroid outbursts and distinguish dust- from gas-driven activity by color; and a framework for commensal or simultaneous observing with other facilities (the Dark Energy Camera, DECam; the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope, SOAR; the Very Large Telescope, VLT; LS4; radio: Simons Observatory, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, ACT; the Square Kilometre Array, SKA) would enable science requiring same-time multi-wavelength coverage (explicitly excluding multi-messenger triggers, which are Group D’s domain).

## IV Group C: Narrow- and Medium-band Surveys and Alternative Filters

Raichoor, A. Rasmussen, M. Redden, L. Sajkov, B. Sherwin, S. Thomas, C.-H. To, H. I. Ullah, C. Williams, M. Yamamoto.

Group C examined multiple ways of changing Rubin’s filter complement beyond the Sloan-heritage $ugrizy$ set (which is optimized for photo- $z$ near $z\sim 0.2$ ): medium-band filters ( $\lambda/\Delta\lambda\sim 15$ –20, $\sim$ 200–800 Å wide) for photometric redshifts, high- $z$ cosmology, AGN reverberation mapping, and stellar archaeology; narrow-band filters for emission-line and biosignature-proxy surveys; “offset” broad bands shifted in wavelength relative to $ugrizy$ while preserving depth and cadence; and more exotic hardware concepts (ramp filters, a segmented “butcher-block” tiled filter array, and exploitation of the bandpass–angle-of-incidence coupling of Rubin’s telecentric design). A recurring observation was that essentially every proposal costs of order one to a few million dollars per filter, a small marginal cost on an existing facility. The unifying proposed was the ratio $R(T,)=\mathrm{FoM}(\text{new filter set})/\mathrm{FoM}(ugrizy)$ at fixed time $T$ and . The seven cases below are summarized here; each is developed in full, with quantitative forecasts, figures, and references, in the group’s detailed document [11].

### IV.1 Cosmology and extragalactic science

#### High-redshift large-scale structure with medium bands

The goal is to measure high-redshift large-scale structure using Lyman- $\alpha$ emitters (LAEs) at $z\gtrsim 2$ selected with medium-band filters, together with LSST-selected Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs) refined by medium-band photometry, and to perform a $2\times 2$ -point analysis (LAE/LBG clustering $\times$ cosmic microwave background, CMB, lensing) constraining $\Omega_{M}$ , $S_{8}$ , neutrino mass, and $(w_{0},w_{a})$ with the longest available lever arm, while accessing primordial-Universe physics ( $f_{\rm NL}$ ) where structure is less nonlinear. The headline figure of merit is a forecast $\sim$ 4–5% constraint on $\sigma_{8}$ per medium band from the LAE clustering $\times$ Simons Observatory CMB-lensing cross-correlation, well beyond existing measurements at this redshift. Only Rubin can detect LAEs and enable clean LBG selection over the $\geq$ 11,000 deg2 that Spec-S5 requires: , the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) has a much smaller , and Subaru/Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) surveys $\sim$ 3 $\times$ more slowly and is not survey-dedicated. The concrete need is a minimal set of $\sim$ 7 medium bands with $\lambda/\Delta\lambda\sim 20$ spanning $2.1\lesssim z\lesssim 3.5$ with continuous coverage (LAE wavelength–redshift mapping: 400 nm $\rightarrow z=2.3$ ; 700 nm $\rightarrow z=4.8$ ), at $\sim$ $1M per filter, ideally reaching $2<z<6.5$ with Roman supplementing the high end. Current target-selection efficiency with plus HSC broadbands is already 75% against DESI. The case connects tightly to the Simons Observatory (SO; which supplies the CMB-lensing map), DESI, and the Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS), and, most importantly, to Spec-S5, whose LAE sample requires $\sim$ 4 years of Rubin dark-time medium-band observing as a precursor: the two facilities should be optimized jointly. The precursor HSC-Niji survey (medium bands binned into four “quadrants” MBQ1–4 to avoid slow filter exchanges; MBQ1 delivered in 2025) demonstrates the approach, and photo- $z$ forecasts indicate that adding $\sim$ 16 medium bands to the six broad bands meets LSST Year 1 (Y1; and largely Year 10, Y10) weak-lensing and large-scale-structure (LSS) photo- $z$ requirements. The chief open question is quantify the marginal gain over LSST alone.

#### Offset broad bands for photometric redshifts

Rather than medium bands, this case adds a set of 5–7 broad bands offset in wavelength from $ugrizy$ , gaining spectral information (and thus better per-object photo- $z$ and high- $z$ target selection) while still retaining the depth needed for transient and proper-motion science that medium bands would sacrifice. The target is a factor of $\sim$ 2 reduction in photo- $z$ scatter and outlier rate, matching the gain expected from doubling spectral resolution and exposure time, at $1–2M per filter. An empirical test using the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) 2020 catalog found that 11 offset broad bands outperform both the six-broadband and the twelve-medium-band scenarios in photo- $z$ scatter and outlier fraction, and a hybrid (six medium blue $+$ six broad) is nearly as good. Because it preserves time-domain science, this is regarded as the “workhorse” filter option; it connects to Spec-S5 target selection, CMB cluster surveys (South Pole Telescope, SPT-3G $+$ /SO), X-ray clusters (Athena), and radio weak lensing (SKA). The prior is synthetic photometry from COSMOS-class spectral-energy-distribution (SED) catalogs rather than new data.

#### AGN accretion-disk reverberation mapping and cosmology

Rubin will produce the largest homogeneous time-domain AGN sample ever assembled, turning continuum reverberation mapping from a targeted, single-quasar technique into a population-scale experiment across black-hole mass, accretion rate, and redshift. Medium bands ( $\lambda/\Delta\lambda\sim 15$ –20) placed to separate continuum-dominated from line-dominated spectral regions, on a $\sim$ 1–2 day cadence in the Deep Drilling Fields, would measure accretion-disk sizes and temperature profiles after removing redshift-dependent contamination, resolving the long-standing puzzle that measured disks are larger than thin-disk theory predicts. A contamination-controlled disk-size sample could in principle serve as a geometric cosmological ruler complementing Type Ia supernovae. A pilot would target continuum lags for several hundred AGN; the mature program, several thousand. The case has natural Chilean co-leadership through Rubin, Gemini-South, and SOAR, with the Southern Photometric Local Universe Survey (S-PLUS) and 4MOST-ChANGES as tie-ins.

#### Protocluster assembly

A companion extragalactic case seeks a complete catalog of protoclusters at $z<4$ , tracing when the highest-mass halos assemble and how their galaxies transform, using precise medium-band or variable-filter photometric redshifts and intracluster light as a mass proxy, building on Euclid, Euclid $\times$ LSST, and Sunyaev–Zel’dovich candidate lists (LSST broadbands alone reach only $z\lesssim 1.3$ –1.4).

### IV.2 Local-Universe, stellar, emission-line, and exotic-filter concepts

#### Galactic archaeology and local dark matter

A set of $\sim$ 5 medium bands ( $\sim$ 200 Å wide; a minimal set is Ca ii H&K plus Mg $b$ ) sensitive to stellar metallicity and surface gravity would map Local Group structure and formation over $\geq$ 70% of the sky, identifying streams, tidally stripped stars, and rare low-metallicity stars, and delivering a 3D distance map to the Milky Way’s virial radius, a probe of small-scale dark matter and first-star enrichment. The target is [Fe/H] to $\sim$ 10% and 90% dwarf/giant discrimination at $g\leq 25$ . Offset broad bands are shown to be insufficient here: the target features have equivalent widths of only $\sim$ 5–10 Å, requiring true medium bands even for faint stars. The transient-cadence cost (a 200 Å band needs $\sim$ 150 s versus 30 s to stay background-limited) is mitigated by making exposure time a function of filter wavelength. IBIS, Niji, and DESI Run 2 are the precursors that will validate the method.

#### Extended-baseline proper motions for halo dark matter

This is a case to probe the distribution of dark matter in the Milky Way halo through the kinematics of satellite dwarf galaxies, globular clusters, and stellar streams, in particular by detecting and modeling the gaps in tidal streams thought to be produced by encounters with dark-matter subhalos, thereby constraining the subhalo mass function. Because proper-motion accuracy improves as $t^{-3/2}$ with time baseline, continuing the survey past 2036 yields large astrometric gains: extending proper-motion accuracy to better than 0.5 mas yr-1 at or below $r\approx 24$ over the entire southern sky. Rubin will already have built a decade-long baseline over an area larger than Roman’s, and to depths not reached by planned astrometric surveys such as GaiaNIR, so additional epochs . : roughly ten to twenty broad-band epochs per year suffice to keep the baseline growing while allowing outlier rejection, and this case is the strongest argument for keeping some fraction of the post-LSST cadence in broad bands (the existing $ugrizy$ or the “offset” broad bands above) rather than moving entirely to medium or narrow bands, which motivates its placement in Group C. The prerequisite is a demonstration, using Gaia as a prior, that LSST can measure proper motions to the required accuracy for faint, low-proper-motion sources, plausibly by DR1 but perhaps requiring a longer baseline. It connects to the offset-broad-band and Galactic-archaeology cases above and to near-field cosmology programs.

#### Narrow-band H $\alpha$ emission-line imaging

An H $\alpha$ survey science from supernova remnants to the star-forming filaments of large-scale structure, bridging to 4MOST spectroscopy, exploiting Rubin’s unique combination of the widest field of view and active-optics-driven uniform image quality. It needs an H $\alpha$ filter or two ramp filters within the existing broadband range (potentially the largest narrow-band filter yet built), with DR1 setting the achievable redshift depth (focus on $z<1$ ); a possible Chilean tie-in is 4MOST-CHANCES.

#### Biosignature-proxy and Kuiper-belt-object triage

Two physics-based “triage” cases (explicitly not claims of detection) ask whether a single well-placed band sharpens a population-scale search. The first tests whether a $\sim$ 710 nm medium band (full width at half maximum, FWHM, 20–40 nm), $r$ and $i$ , can flag a vegetation-red-edge-like reflectance feature and separate it from haze/methane look-alikes, reducing the number of stacked detections needed to reach $3\sigma$ – $5\sigma$ ; the second tests whether a $\sim$ 450 nm blue-visible medium band (FWHM $\approx$ 60–80 nm) improves separation of organic-rich, ice-rich, mixed, and weakly active Kuiper-belt-object surface states beyond $ugrizy$ (figure of merit: $\geq$ 25% gain in the pairwise Mahalanobis distance at fixed cost). Both are framed as that concentrate scarce spectroscopy on the highest-information targets, and both to weather (near-simultaneous color pairs) and satellite-megaconstellation trails in the blue.

#### Exotic filter hardware

Three hardware concepts round out the group. The “butcher-block” segmented filter array would bond 21 uniform narrow-band tiles, one per charge-coupled-device (CCD) raft, into a single 75 cm element, giving each raft a clean, non-smeared bandpass the fast-beam smearing problem, sampling $\sim$ 21 redshift slices in one exposure with dithering (precedents: NASA “butcher-block” arrays, PAUCam). Leveraging the bandpass–angle-of-incidence covariance, explicitly a generic technique, not a science case, uses masks on the primary mirror to shift bandpasses by $|\Delta\lambda/\lambda|\approx 0.01$ using existing glass, exploiting Rubin’s telecentric coupling of pupil radius to incidence angle (14.1∘–23.5∘). And “ramp” (spatially variable) filters recur as the favored configuration for the protocluster and H $\alpha$ cases, with the caveat that their feasibility and the required new data-processing pipeline remain to be demonstrated. A shared implication across all of these is that current pipelines assume a discrete, unchanging filter set, so non-standard filters would require new data-processing pipelines, a substantial but tractable development effort.

## VI Group E: Enabling Technology and Upgrades

Group E was concerned with the instrumental capabilities underpinning the scientific opportunities discussed by the other groups. Proposed modifications were organized into three tiers by cost, risk, and lead time. The discussion focused on hardware modifications, though algorithmic advancements and on-summit edge computing were discussed briefly. Two physical constraints were important: (1) Rubin’s fast $f/1.2$ beam limits how narrow or spatially variable a filter can be, and (2) the camera is modular electronically but not mechanically, so even a single-raft swap requires the costly operation of opening the cryostat. Several system configuration changes were identified that could be implemented almost immediately to provide novel capabilities. Moderate upgrades were perceived to be possible to implement on the mid-2030s timeline, and the design and fabrication of a new filter set was perceived to have the largest marginal science gain per dollar. Major upgrades were discussed briefly, since they were not perceived to be viable on a mid-2030s timeline.

The scope of Group E overlaps Group C (filters) and underpins Groups A, B, and D (image quality, fast readout, on-summit compute). This section is best read as a summary of the technical capabilities that could enable the scientific roadmaps described in the other sections. The full tier-by-tier discussion, together with the group’s appendices summarized in §VI.4, is given in its detailed document [4].

### VI.1 Tier 1: configuration-only changes (months–1 yr, software/configuration/calibration)

Several new capabilities require no procurement, only new operating modes, calibration, and software, and can be interspersed with survey operations using hardware that already exists (a spare ITL raft at SLAC, , a spare shutter). These include readout-mode changes (current 3.3 s at 5–6 e- rms; 2.2 s demonstrated within noise spec; row-binning to $0.2\times 0.4$ arcsec2 pixels nearly doubles readout speed); a region-of-interest (ROI) “guider” mode (design $50\times 50$ pixels/amp at 9 Hz; $\sim$ 80 Mpix across the focal plane at 5 Hz); open-shutter, continuous-readout ( $\sim$ 10 ms effective temporal resolution) and stuttered readout (effective frame rates $\sim$ 20 Hz); a no-filter “light bucket” mode; and recoating the combined primary/tertiary mirror (M1M3) to improve $u$ -band throughput, where Rubin is most photon-starved. Together these fast-transient, FRB-counterpart, AGN-variability, Milky-Way GW-counterpart, and $\sim$ 10–100 ms compact-object light-curve science, directly serving Groups B and D, and the group flagged them as the fastest, lowest-risk items on the whole list.

### VI.2 Tier 2: moderate upgrades ($10M–$100M, $\sim$ 5 yr R&D + $\sim$ 5 yr build)

#### Alternative filter sets.

A new filter complement was perceived as an avenue to deliver high-impact science on a timescale that could be commensurate with the end of LSST. The technical viability of several different alternative filter sets was discussed. Rubin’s fast $f/1.2$ beam was of central importance in these discussions. This fast beam spreads the light from a point source over a $\sim$ 12 cm ( $\sim$ 100 cm2) footprint on the filter, or conversely, a point on the filter surface is spread over $\sim$ 12 cm on the focal plane. In addition, the incident angle for the fast beam ranges from $\sim$ 14∘–23∘, thereby limiting the minimum bandwidth of a filter. Together, these features limit both the minimum bandpass and spatial resolution.

Offset broad bands ( $\sim$ 5 filters, $\sim$ 100–150 nm wide) are the most straightforward, along with a single “light bucket” extra-broad filter; a medium-band set (dividing each broad band into 4–5 bands, IBIS/Niji-like, $\sim$ $15–20M) plausibly deliver a factor-of- $\sim$ 2 improvement in photo- $z$ scatter plus emission-line and stellar-population capability, all mounting into the existing filter exchanger with no focal-plane redesign.

Narrow bands (feasible down to $\sim$ 15–20 nm, not $\sim$ 8 nm) were disfavored due to low throughput but may be considered if motivated by science cases. Notable variants were also proposed, including “comb filters” comprised of combinations of medium-band filters, a broad “light bucket” filter, and “one filter to rule them all” using a single, deliberately non-uniform (segmented, linear, or radial; offset, broad, medium, narrow, or comb) filter to build differential spectra of every object. The binding constraint on both tame and exotic filter proposals is manufacturability, not optical design (the fast beam and the vendor experience with the original filters), which a bounded vendor design study, paired with quantitative photo- $z$ image simulations using public tools such as , tasked to Group C, can retire.

#### Other moderate upgrades.

The group a faster shutter (the current shutter opens or closes in $\sim$ 0.9 s nominal, Johnson 25; a spare “B-unit” exists; $\sim$ 0.3 s achievable with modest safety engineering, 0.1 s as a purpose-built stretch goal); a single-raft detector replacement as both standalone science (one raft subtends $\sim$ 40 arcmin, enough for a fast Galactic-plane survey) and a pathfinder for a future focal-plane upgrade, with options spanning fast single-layer poly-Si CCDs ( $\sim$ 10 fps), low-noise MAS Skipper/SiSeRO devices, complementary-metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensors, and near-infrared (NIR)-sensitive Ge CCDs (to $\sim$ 1.4 µm) or InGaAs ; ground-layer adaptive optics via an actuated secondary (M2 GLAO), targeting $\sim$ 0.5 arcsec delivered image quality across the 3.5∘ field; a tunable-laser satellite calibrator in the spirit of (part of PIONEER program), and an AuxTel upgrade to reach the sub-nanometer bandpass knowledge that supernova cosmology and any new narrow/medium-band filter set will require; and GPU edge computing on the summit for a $\sim$ 1–3 s alert stream, real-time classification and ToO triggering (e.g., LISA follow-up), and information-driven dynamic scheduling, described as the lowest-risk item with the weakest dependencies on the other options.

### VI.3 Tier 3: major upgrades ($100M+, multi-year downtime)

The most ambitious options brieflybut detailed discussion was deferred due to the long to deployment: a full focal-plane detector replacement (which necessarily begins with a pathfinder raft that itself delivers science); mounting filters immediately in front of the detectors to defeat the 12 cm beam-footprint problem (which changes, rather than eliminates, the filter-design problem because the beam is not telecentric at the focal plane); a redesign of the camera and optics to perform a near-infrared wide-fast-deep survey; and a spectroscopic instrument (a single raft of integral-field units, which 100 µm fibers would need $\sim$ 1 M fibers and many spectrographs), considered only because , and with the strong caveat that spectroscopy would surrender Rubin’s defining advantage of wide-field, fast-slewing time-domain imaging.

Rather than a single recommendation, the group distilled its discussion into a set of concrete, near-term actionable items with indicative owners and lead times: bounded, fundable studies that could begin now to inform the Astro2030 process. ## VIII Conclusion

The Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop gathered community participants around the question: more than a decade of prior community planning (Appendix D) and to prepare well-developed science cases for the next decadal survey (Astro2030). Although the LSST began only in 2026, the long lead times of any facility change, from cadence and filters to focal-plane hardware, mean that it is not too early to start this process now. The overarching is that Rubin’s étendue will remain unmatched through the 2030s, so continuing to operate and evolve the facility a high-return, best-available investment rather than a marginal extension.

The five groups reached the following main conclusions:

- • Group A (continued LSST-style surveying): a deeper, extended survey pays off only if the faint, crowded sky can be measured, so the priority is sustained investment in data-analysis software, computing, and machine-learning infrastructure, such as survey-native foundation models, rather than in new hardware (Section II; Yadav 35).

- • Group B (alternative cadences and footprints): a flexible, proposal-driven process (a “metacase”) for allocating post-LSST time is the natural organizing framework, enabling science-driven cadences from a Milky-Way exoplanet-transit census to Type Ia supernova cosmology, time-delay cosmography, and second-scale transients (Section III; Birrer and others 10).

- • Group C (narrow- and medium-band surveys and filters): new filter sets are the highest-leverage, modest-cost evolution of the hardware, with offset broad bands preserving time-domain science and medium and narrow bands unlocking high-redshift large-scale structure, AGN reverberation mapping, Galactic archaeology, and emission-line science (Section IV; Bleem and others 11).

- • Group D (targets of opportunity and multi-messenger): extending Rubin’s demonstrated target-of-opportunity system into the gravitational-wave and neutrino era it the premier engine for multi-messenger cosmology and astrophysics, at a modest fraction of observing time (Section V; MacBride and others 28).

- • Group E (enabling technology and upgrades): the instrumental options fall into configuration-only changes available now and moderate upgrades feasible on the mid-2030s timeline, with a new filter complement offering the largest science return per dollar (Section VI; Allen et al. 4).

Cross-cutting priorities recurred throughout, including opportunities for Chilean and Latin-American co-leadership (Section VII), the impact of weather and climate at Cerro Pachón, the effect of satellite megaconstellations, and the programmatic reality that any post-LSST program must make a compelling case to multiple funding agencies and sources within the facility’s operating-cost envelope. ## Appendix D Prior Community Efforts

This workshop builds on more than a decade of community planning on the future of Rubin/LSST after its main survey. We summarize that lineage here; a consistent thread is that Rubin/LSST is a facility to be evolved, not retired, and that the concrete decision among “continue as-is / modest filter change / new instrument” should take into consideration results from on-sky LSST data.

#### The Cosmic Visions Dark Energy Panel (2016–2018).

Convened by DOE High Energy Physics after the 2014 Particle Physics Project Prioritization Panel (P5) report, the CVDE panel held community workshops at the University of Chicago (September 2016) and LBNL (November 2017) and produced linked reports on the science [18] and the enabling technology [19], followed by a Small Projects Portfolio [17]. Together they framed the completion of Stage-IV surveys (DESI, LSST) as a launching point rather than an endpoint, arguing that great cosmological information remains at $z>1$ and on nonlinear scales, and proposed a moderate-cost portfolio including complementary spectroscopy and narrow-/offset-broad-band imaging to sharpen LSST photometric redshifts. This is the intellectual origin of the “Stage V” framing later adopted by Snowmass.

#### The 2019 Argonne Next-generation Instrumentation Workshop.

The first dedicated technical workshop on what hardware follows LSSTCam [34] mapped three evolution pathways: continued imaging (possibly with new $\sim$ 20 nm narrow-band filters), an alternative-sensor focal plane (microwave kinetic inductance detectors, MKIDs; germanium CCDs; InGaAs for near-IR reach), or conversion to a massively multiplexed ( $\sim$ 30,000-fiber) multi-object spectrograph, and concluded, without advocacy, that new filters are the cheapest near-term option while cryogenic IR focal planes are currently cost-prohibitive. Its cost/performance/risk taxonomy recurs throughout the later literature and in Group E of this workshop.

#### The Astro2020 Decadal white papers (2019).

Two Astro2020 submissions addressed the question directly. “Next Generation LSST Science” [24] laid out the continue/modify/replace scenarios, argued LSST’s imaging étendue will remain scientifically premier well past ten years (especially for dynamic-sky science), and called for a mid-decade community process. “Future Uses of the LSST Facility” [26], a non-advocacy assessment by the LSST Project Science Team, quantified how coadded depth, photometric precision, and parallax/proper-motion accuracy continue to improve past year 10 and estimated the extended-operations cost. A companion Astro2020 white paper made the specific science case for adding $\sim$ 15–20 nm narrow-band filters to Rubin [36], for stellar astrophysics, emission-line nebulae, and improved photometric redshifts, the direct precedent for much of Group C.

#### Snowmass 2021.

The dedicated Snowmass white paper “Rubin Observatory after LSST” [12] restated the three-scenario framework and worked through the science drivers (dark energy beyond $w_{0}$ – $w_{a}$ , gravity and dark-matter tests, the $H_{0}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ tensions, strong-lensing cosmography, GW/kilonova follow-up, dwarf-satellite proper motions, Roman/Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) synergy), recommending the case be revisited by year 5 of the survey. The Cosmic Frontier topical-group reports reinforced this: the complementarity report [21] formally advocated continued Rubin operation after LSST alongside DESI-II, CMB-S4, and a Stage-V spectroscopic facility, and the Cosmic Frontier 04 (CF04) report [6], whose §4.5 is titled “Opportunity: The Rubin Observatory after LSST,” gave the most detailed menu, escalating from continuing as-is, to re-surveying with half-bandwidth-offset filters (roughly halving photo- $z$ errors), to a 20–30-band low-resolution “filter spectrograph” ( $\sigma_{z}\sim 0.005(1+z)$ ), to a full camera replacement, and stated that it was premature to choose among them before 1–2 years of LSST data.

#### Recurring recommendations.

Across all of these efforts the same conclusions recur: (i) Rubin should be evolved, not retired, given its unmatched étendue; (ii) a standard continue/modify-filters/replace-instrument menu; (iii) narrow-, medium-, and offset-broad-band filters as the most consistently recommended modest-cost path; (iv) the intrinsic value of a longer time baseline (proper motions, parallaxes, depth) independent of any hardware change; (v) a massively multiplexed spectrograph as the recurring ‘‘big’’ option, now largely externalized to Spec-S5; and (vi) deferral of the final decision until real survey data are in hand. Practical resources compiled for participants include the Rubin survey-strategy documentation66 6 https://survey-strategy.lsst.io and the HSC medium-band filter specifications77 7 https://sites.google.com/view/hsc-mb-workshop/filter-specification.
